content: Healthcare in the Republic of Ireland is regulated under the Health Act of 2004, which led to the creation of the Health Service Executive (HSE), a centralized body responsible for managing the national health service. The HSE officially began operations on January 1, 2005, although its organizational structures are still being developed. Hospital care is universally free for all residents. Additionally, individuals and their dependents who fall below a specific income threshold, or meet other qualifying criteria, are eligible for a medical card, which grants access to additional free services such as dental care, hearing and oral care, prescription medications, and general practitioner (GP) visits. The Minister for Health and Children is tasked with setting overarching policies for the healthcare system. The HSE, as a single national entity, oversees the delivery of all healthcare services. While the Health Boards that previously managed healthcare no longer exist as independent entities, their structures have been integrated into the HSE as regional divisions. Each former health board area now functions as a division of the HSE, with the former chief executive officers of these boards serving as chief officers for their respective HSE regions. The HSE employs approximately 120,000 staff members. Once the HSE's reorganization is complete, the system will be divided into three main directorates. The National Hospitals Office will oversee hospital services through a network of hospital groups. The Primary, Community, and Continuing Care Directorate will manage community-based healthcare services, which will be further divided into four Regional Health Offices. Lastly, the National Shared Services Centre will handle administrative and support functions. Healthcare delivery in Ireland is a significant political issue, as the system operates through a combination of public and private services. The system has been criticized for being fragmented and lacking coordination, which prevents it from achieving economies of scale. Private health insurance is available for those who wish to purchase it, with providers such as Vhi Healthcare, BUPA Ireland, and VIVAS Health offering coverage. Critics argue that Vhi Healthcare has used the debate over risk equalization to maintain its market dominance by seeking substantial payments from its competitor, BUPA Ireland. Under the General Medical Services (GMS) scheme, free primary healthcare is provided to individuals below a certain income level and to all individuals over the age of 70, regardless of income. Those eligible for the scheme receive a medical card issued by the HSE. However, this system has been criticized for being reactive, focusing on treating illnesses rather than preventing them. There is ongoing advocacy to expand the medical card scheme to cover the entire population. A large portion of the population is either covered by private health insurance or the GMS scheme. Meanwhile, many employed individuals contribute to the healthcare system through the Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI) system, which is managed by the state but offers limited benefits. Primary healthcare in Ireland is predominantly provided by general practitioners (GPs), who typically operate as sole practitioners or in small group practices with one or two other GPs and, occasionally, practice nurses. GPs generally charge patients on a per-visit basis, although individuals with medical cards are exempt from these fees. The structure of GP practices in Ireland has been criticized for its lack of integration with other medical disciplines, such as pediatric, dental, and community care services. These services are often provided in separate facilities, even in small towns or villages, which can make access less convenient for patients. Hospitals in Ireland are typically operated as voluntary organizations managed by trusts or foundations. However, some hospitals, such as James Connolly Memorial Hospital in Blanchardstown, are directly managed by the HSE. Teaching hospitals are often affiliated with universities and provide both medical education and patient care. Most hospitals in Ireland offer a comprehensive range of services, including accident and emergency care. A contentious issue in Irish healthcare is the proposal to restructure hospital services, with some local hospitals potentially offering only specific services while larger hospitals provide a full spectrum of care. This proposal has sparked significant political debate.
